questions.q: In `for (Integer i = 0; i < 5; i++) { ... }`, how many times does the loop body run, and with what values of i?
options: Six times, with i equal to 0 through 5
Five times, with i equal to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 -- the loop stops once i reaches 5, before that iteration runs
Four times, with i equal to 1, 2, 3, 4
An unlimited number of times, since no stopping point is defined
questions.explain: The lesson walks through this exact example: the condition i < 5 becomes false once i reaches 5, so the loop runs for i = 0 through 4, five iterations total, not six.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a `while` loop and a `do while` loop, per this lesson?
options: A while loop checks its condition before the first iteration and may run zero times; a do while loop checks its condition after the first iteration, guaranteeing at least one run
A do while loop can never run more than once
A while loop always runs at least once, just like do while
There is no functional difference between the two
questions.explain: The lesson states a while loop checks its condition before running and may run zero times if the condition starts false, while a do while loop checks after running, guaranteeing the body executes at least once.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a `for each` loop over a counting `for` loop when looping over every item in a collection?
options: A for each loop runs faster in every case
A for each loop removes the risk of an off-by-one counting mistake, since it runs automatically once per item with no counter or condition to manage
A counting for loop cannot be used with collections under any circumstances
A for each loop requires writing more code than a counting for loop
questions.explain: The lesson notes that a for each loop reads naturally and has no counter to manage or condition to get wrong, specifically removing the off-by-one risk that counting for loops are prone to.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of an infinite loop, per this lesson?
options: Using a for each loop instead of a counting for loop
Forgetting to update the variable that the loop's stopping condition depends on, so the condition never becomes false
Declaring too many variables inside the loop body
Using System.debug inside a loop
questions.explain: The lesson's infinite-loop example shows a while loop where the increment (count++) was forgotten, so the condition count < 5 never becomes false and the loop never stops -- the most common cause the lesson identifies.

questions.q: What habit does this lesson recommend to avoid writing an infinite loop?
options: Never use while loops, only for loops
Always use a do while loop instead of a while loop
Every time you write a loop condition, ask what inside the loop makes that condition eventually false, and confirm it happens on every iteration with no skipped path
Add a System.debug statement to every loop
questions.explain: The lesson's explicit recommendation is to ask, for every loop condition, what inside the loop makes it eventually false, and to confirm that actually happens on every iteration without exception.
